doc.title: Junior Mance Part I interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, New York City, New York, July 27, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Accompanying Joe Williams and Dinah Washington
summary: Working with vocalists, Joe Williams with his trio under John Levy, and Dinah Washington's perfect pitch.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Joe Williams: the singer with Basie

blocks.x: Can we move up in your career to the time you were playing with some of the great vocalists. You’ve accompanied Dinah Washington, and Joe Williams — © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-
Dinah Washington, Joe Williams, Johnny Hartman, Jimmy Rushing, Jimmy Witherspoon. Those are the main ones I think, that I remember.
What was it like working with Joe?

With Joe it was great. I knew Joe from Chicago anyway, Joe lived, I think he grew up in Chicago, he was born in Georgia. And it was a good experience working with Joe. I had my trio working with Joe, which was Bob Cranshaw and Mickey Roker and myself. And we had a good time. We had the same manager, John Levy, and he thought it was a good idea to put the two together, to solve two things. We usually played a short set before Joe came on and then played for Joe. And that was a good experience. I really liked working with Joe. Joe I think is one of the most, well he’s well-known now, but even back then I think he was very under rated. Because so many other guys were just going beyond him, I mean in popularity I’m talking about. And they tried to brand him as a blues singer, which he didn’t want, but he can sing the blues, I love to hear him sing the blues. But he knows how to do everything. He’s a good ballad singer. In fact I remember, this was when Mike Douglas had his T.V. show and it was coming out of Cleveland then. And we did the show and then we were watching the show after it was taped, and we were watching in the credits in the beginning and it said blah blah blah, different artists, and featuring blues singer Joe Williams. And he hit the ceiling. He didn’t like it. He wanted to be known as an all-around singer. But at that time, this was coming off, he was just coming out of the Basie band and he’d had those big hits, “Every Day,” and “All Right OK You Win” and that’s what made him, really. That’s what John Levy used to try to tell him. But I had no problems with Joe or with Dinah. You know everybody is always asking me, “How did you get along with Dinah?” Great. I had no problems with her. Wynton Kelly had no problems with her. I followed Wynton Kelly on two jobs, with Dinah and with Dizzy. Yeah, Wynton was a buddy. But I never had any problems with Dinah. She gave me complete freedom as to how to play behind her. Like I say sometimes she would sit down and show me certain chords that she would like. The amazing thing about Dinah, Dinah had perfect pitch. There were some tunes she would want to start just cold with no intro, and maybe the tune before that was in an entirely different key. And she never missed. In the two years I worked with her, she never missed. Cannonball also had perfect pitch. Because he and Nat, Nat had relative — is that what they call it — and they used to make these little side bets. You know if a car horn passed, and we were sitting in the barracks or something, anyway, Cannon would say B flat. And Nat said no, no, no, no, no, that’s B natural or A natural. It would be close. Cannon was always right. But Nat was close enough.
